theme: David’s victories; the census; preparing for the Temple
readingInstruction: Read 1 Chronicles 18:1-22:19. David’s victories are summarized, and the book tells of his census sin and the choice of the temple site. David then prepares for the temple he will not build. Notice what the Chronicler leaves out.
settingTheScene: The Chronicler summarizes David’s wars in a single chapter or two, and he leaves out the story of Bathsheba and Uriah entirely. This is not a cover-up, since the readers knew Samuel and Kings. His purpose is different. He wants to show the faithful side of David and focus on the temple. The one sin he does include is the census, because it led to the site of the temple.
observation: “And the LORD gave victory to David wherever he went” (18:6).
“Satan stood against Israel and incited David to number Israel” (21:1).
“But the king’s word prevailed against Joab” (21:4).
“And God was displeased with this thing, and he struck Israel” (21:7).
“I have sinned greatly in that I have done this thing. But now, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly” (21:8).
“Let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is very great, but let me not fall into the hand of man” (21:13).
“But I will buy it for the full price. I will not take for the LORD what is yours, nor offer a burnt offering that costs me nothing” (21:24).
“Here shall be the house of the LORD God and here the altar of burnt offering for Israel” (22:1).
interpretation:
The Chronicler selects. He tells us about David’s victories and his order of mighty men, but not about the affair with Bathsheba. He includes the census, a sin that brought a plague upon Israel and killed 70,000 people. Why this one? Because the story ends with David buying the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, where he sees the angel of the LORD stand with a drawn sword. That place becomes the site of the temple. Out of the worst moment of David’s reign, God brings forth the place where sacrifices will be offered for the sin of the people.

It begins in a surprising way: “Satan stood against Israel and incited David.” The parallel in 2 Samuel 24 says the anger of the LORD incited David. The Chronicler preserves both: God allows the adversary to test, and God’s purposes are served. David’s sin is pride in numbers: he is relying on his army, not on God. When he recognizes his guilt, he confesses honestly. He does not blame Joab, who objected. And when given the choice of punishments, David says, “Let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is very great.” Even in judgment, he trusts God’s character more than any human hand.

At the threshing floor, Ornan offers to give the land free. But David says, “I will not offer a burnt offering that costs me nothing.” Real worship costs. David pays full price. And the fire from heaven answers his offering.

Chapter 22 shows David preparing materials for the temple, though God says Solomon, a man of rest, will build it because David has shed much blood. David accepts it. He gathers gold, silver, iron, bronze, and timber “in great quantities” for the son who will build. This is a picture of a person who works for what he will not see finished.
connection: Hebrews 10:1-14 says the repeated sacrifices could not take away sin, but Christ offered himself once for all. 2 Samuel 24:24 is the parallel verse about costly offerings. Romans 12:1 says to present our bodies as a living sacrifice. 1 Peter 1:18-19 says we were ransomed with the precious blood of Christ. Matthew 6:21: where your treasure is, there your heart will be. Genesis 22:2 mentions Mount Moriah, linked to this site in 2 Chronicles 3:1.
application:
Ask whether any of your giving or service “costs you nothing.” What would it look like to give something that costs?

Remember David’s choice: when you fail, fall into the hands of the LORD, for his mercy is great.

Prepare for something you will not see completed, a ministry, a legacy, or a gift for the next generation.
prayerPrompts: Confess sin to God honestly and ask him to take away your iniquity.
Tell him you trust his mercy.
Thank him for the altar and the sacrifice.
